nameStory: The Small White gets its name from being the smaller cousin of the Large White butterfly, both appearing as delicate white flutters in gardens. In North America, it's more commonly called the Cabbage White because its caterpillars have an infamous appetite for cabbage, broccoli, kale, and other garden crops in the mustard family. This little butterfly earned its 'small' designation to distinguish it from its bigger, more aggressive relative that can cause even more garden mayhem.
description: The Small White is a delicate, small-to-medium sized butterfly with bright white wings decorated with small black spots and markings. Its wings span about 1.5-2 inches across, making it noticeably smaller than many other white butterflies you'll encounter. The males typically show one black spot on each forewing, while females display two spots, and both sexes have subtle black markings along the wing edges. This common butterfly flutters through gardens, fields, and anywhere its favorite mustard family plants grow, often appearing almost paper-like as it dances from flower to flower.

idTips.label: Wing spots
idTips.description: Look for small, round black spots on the white forewings - males have one spot per wing, females have two spots per wing that look like tiny black buttons against the white background

idTips.label: Wing tips
idTips.description: The wing tips show gray or black markings that look like someone lightly dusted them with charcoal, much subtler than the bold black bands of larger white butterflies

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Noticeably smaller than a Large White butterfly, with a delicate, almost fragile appearance as it flutters - about the size of a large coin when wings are spread

idTips.label: Underwing color
idTips.description: The undersides of the wings appear yellowish or pale green-white, especially on the hindwings, giving them a soft, muted appearance when at rest

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Flies with a gentle, bouncing flutter that looks almost erratic, like a small piece of paper caught in a breeze, staying close to garden plants

habitat: Small Whites thrive in gardens, agricultural areas, parks, and disturbed habitats throughout New England, especially where cabbage family plants grow. You'll find them in vegetable gardens, along roadsides, in weedy lots, and around farms from sea level to moderate elevations. They're particularly drawn to areas with wild mustards, garden brassicas like cabbage and broccoli, and flowering plants that provide nectar.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, with the first generation appearing in May. Look for them visiting early wildflowers and beginning to lay eggs on young mustard family plants.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs through summer with multiple overlapping generations. Adults are most abundant and easily spotted visiting flowers and laying eggs on garden crops during warm, sunny days.
seasonality.fall: Final generation emerges in early fall, with adults continuing to fly until the first hard frosts. Late-season individuals may appear slightly larger and darker than summer butterflies.
seasonality.winter: Overwinters as a chrysalis (pupae) attached to plant stems or garden structures. No adult activity during winter months in New England.

funFact: This innocent-looking butterfly is actually one of the world's most successful agricultural invaders - it spread from Europe to six different continents in just 200 years, hitchhiking along global trade routes and following human agriculture wherever cabbage-family crops were planted!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with the larger Cabbage White (Large White), but Small Whites are noticeably smaller with more delicate black markings and lack the bold black wing tip bands. Remember: 'Small and subtle spots' versus 'Large with loud markings.' Native Mustard Whites and West Virginia Whites appear more translucent and prefer wild woodland habitats rather than gardens.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Cabbage White' in North America, this species is technically the Small White - the true Large White (Cabbage White) is much less common here. Many gardeners know this butterfly's caterpillars as 'imported cabbageworms,' green pests that can quickly skeletonize broccoli and cabbage plants. This is a non-native species that arrived in North America in the 1860s and has become completely naturalized.
compareHints: The Small White differs from its native relatives, the Mustard White and West Virginia White, by having more opaque, bright white wings and distinct black spots rather than the translucent, checkered appearance of the native species. While the native whites prefer woodland edges and wild plants, Small Whites are garden lovers that thrive around human activity. The Small White also flies more persistently in open, sunny areas while native whites tend to stay in shadier, more protected habitats.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike the Small White (an introduced species that's more tolerant of disturbed areas), the mustard white sticks to wilder habitats and shows distinct seasonal forms.
West Virginia Whites differ from their close relatives, the Small White and Mustard White, by their exclusive forest habitat and translucent wing quality.

ecologicalRole.pestNote: Common crop pest — caterpillars damage cabbage family plants
